activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Sociologist Mark Granovetter's 1973 paper 'The Strength of Weak Ties' found that people often learned of new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends.
story:
The removal truck left tire marks in the frost, and Jaxon stood in the driveway of a house he had lived in for exactly four hours, holding a trash bag of packing paper nobody wanted. His mother was inside arguing with a heating system that clicked like a stubborn clock. In the old town, a Saturday like this would have meant the river path with Dev and Marcus, or nothing at all, which was its own kind of luxury: doing nothing with people who already knew you. Here, doing nothing meant doing it alone.

On Monday he walked into his third-period class two minutes late because the hallways of Fairmont High formed a geometry he hadn't decoded yet, and every route seemed to preempt every other route, doubling back on itself. The teacher, Mr. Chea, didn't make a speech about it. He just said, "Jaxon, sit anywhere," and kept writing on the board. Jaxon slid into a seat beside a girl with headphones around her neck, who looked up, decided something about him in half a second, and went back to underlining her notes. Her margins were full of arrows.

"You're the new one," said a boy behind him at the bell. "Rowen. You play anything?" Jaxon said soccer, badly, and Rowen nodded like that was acceptable, like badly was a known quantity. The girl with the headphones turned out to be Annabella, and by Friday she had appointed herself his guide to which cafeteria lines were survivable and which teachers collected grudges. She and Rowen argued constantly, in the comfortable way of people who have never once considered not talking to each other. Jaxon mostly listened. Listening was easy. Belonging to the listening was the part that hadn't happened yet, and he could feel the difference like a draft under a door.

What he wanted, concretely, was money for the spring trip his mother had already said they couldn't cover, and, less concretely, a reason to be somewhere on Saturdays. So when Annabella mentioned that the pharmacy on Delmore Street was hiring, he rode his bike there the same afternoon and filled out a form on a clipboard chained to the counter. The pharmacist glanced at it and said they'd had forty applications. Jaxon rode home with the rejection already arriving in advance, like weather you can see coming across a field.

That weekend his mother sent him to return a casserole dish to the neighbor three doors down, a man he had met exactly twice, once while carrying boxes and once while shoveling the walk. The neighbor, watering dead-looking houseplants on his porch, asked how Jaxon was settling in. Jaxon said fine. Then, because the silence after "fine" was worse than talking, he said he was looking for part-time work. The neighbor set down his watering can. "My sister manages the pharmacy on Delmore," he said. "I'll mention your name Monday."

Walking home with the empty dish, Jaxon turned it over in his head. Dev, his closest friend back home, had sent him twenty job listings over the fall, all of them dead ends, all of them searched for with the loyalty of someone who wanted desperately to help. And here a near-stranger had done in one sentence what two months of close friendship hadn't. In sociology on Tuesday, he typed it into his phone before he could lose it: Mark Granovetter's 1973 paper, "The Strength of Weak Ties," found that people often learned of new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends. He read it twice. It wasn't a complaint about Dev. It was just true, and it reframed the whole fall: his old friends cared about him, and their caring had no new information in it, because they knew everything he knew.

He got the interview on Wednesday and the job on Thursday, Saturdays and two evenings a week, stocking shelves and running the register under a laminated sign about antigens and allergy medication that he was expected to explain to customers by his second month. At lunch he told Annabella and Rowen about the neighbor, expecting them to shrug. Instead Rowen said, "Wait, you barely know that guy," and Annabella said, "That's the whole point, though," and then, finding she couldn't finish the point, looked at Jaxon to finish it for her.

"There's this paper," he said. "Sociologist Mark Granovetter, 1973, 'The Strength of Weak Ties.' He found that people often learned of new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends." He shrugged, embarrassed by his own certainty. "Could be luck, honestly. One data point." Annabella was already leaning forward, saying something about how that was why cities felt cosmopolitan to her, all those half-known faces actually mattering, and Rowen was arguing that his cousin had gotten him his job and cousins were family, so the paper was wrong, or maybe cousins didn't count, and Jaxon felt the argument open around him like a seat being held.

On Saturday he clocked in at nine. The pharmacist handed him a name tag, still warm from the label maker, and pointed at aisle four.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: A 2018 study by Erica Boothby and colleagues found a liking gap: after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company.
story:
Camille arrived eleven minutes early, which she decided was worse than arriving late, because now she had to stand at the counter of the ice cream shop pretending to study the flavors while the boy behind the register watched her not order. She read the list twice. Salted caramel, pistachio, something called Midnight Blackout. Francois had suggested this place by text, with a period at the end, and she had spent two days deciding whether the period meant anything.

He came in at four on the dot, pushing his hair off his forehead. "You got here before me. I'm sorry. The bus."

"It's fine. I just got here." She had not just got there. "Do you know what you want?"

They ordered, and the trouble began at the window seat, small and ordinary: she laughed too loud at his joke about his economics teacher, then worried the laugh had been too loud, and covered it by asking him a serious question about the economy, which was a thing she did when she was nervous. Francois, it turned out, actually liked economics. He talked about stagflation, prices climbing while everything stalled, and she found she wanted to follow it, and that wanting made her quieter than she meant to be.

Then it went wrong in the small ways she would later catalogue. She called pistachio "pistashio," twice, and he corrected her gently the first time and said nothing the second. He mentioned Andres, and she said something dismissive about Andres's party last month, a remark meant to be funny, and felt it land as something meaner, a way of denigrating someone he knew. And when Ms. Mori, her old neighbor, stopped by the table to say hello, Camille was so startled that she barely managed "Hi, nice to see you," in a voice so querulous it came out like a complaint, and Ms. Mori moved on with a careful smile.

Francois paid before she could reach for her wallet. "Next time you get it," he said, and she said "Okay, sure," and then heard herself add, "I mean, if there's a next time," which came out flattened, self-protective, nothing like the joke she intended. His face did something brief and unreadable. They finished their cones. At the corner where they would split directions, he said, "I had a good time," and she said "Yeah, me too," and he said "See you Monday," and walked off toward the river, and she stood there holding her phone and not knowing anything.

She walked home the long way, by the field with the dying goal nets, and did the thing she always did: replayed it. The laugh. The pistashio. The thing about Andres. The flattened joke. He had said "I had a good time," but people said that the way they said "nice to meet you," a door closing politely. By the time she reached her street she had constructed the whole evening from his side, and in that version he had spent forty minutes wishing he were somewhere else.

Her brother was at the kitchen table with his laptop, finishing a psych assignment he'd put off all weekend. She dropped onto the chair across from him and said, "Can I ask you something. If a conversation goes badly, do you know right away?"

He looked up. "What did you do."

"Nothing. Forget it." She got herself water. When she came back he had turned the laptop toward her, and on the screen was a paragraph he'd highlighted for his paper, about a 2018 study by Erica Boothby and her colleagues. She read it twice. After a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company.

"It has a name," her brother said. "The liking gap."

"That's the word? Liking gap."

"That's the word." He turned the laptop back. "It's the whole reason I don't call people after parties."

Camille stood with her glass of water and turned it over. The study didn't say the other person always liked you. It said you usually got the reading wrong, that the gap ran one direction, that her construction of his evening was probably not his evening. Probably. She couldn't know which conversations were the exceptions. She took out her phone, held it, and put it away again, because a text tonight would be a different kind of overcorrecting, and she wanted to get the size of the thing right.

On Monday she came into class early, before the room filled. Francois was already there, headphones half off. She set her bag on the desk beside his.

"Pistachio," she said. "I looked it up. I'd been saying it wrong my whole life, basically."

"Everyone says it wrong the first time," he said, and pulled one headphone fully off. "So there's this thing about stagflation I never got to finish telling you."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Supporters of lowering the US voting age to 18 used the slogan "old enough to fight, old enough to vote," because 18-year-olds could be drafted for the Vietnam War.
story:
The envelope had been on the kitchen counter for nine days, and Nicolas had moved it twice without opening it, once to make room for the groceries and once because he didn't like the way it sat there, official and patient, as if it had nowhere else to be. His ballot. His first. He was eighteen and the vote had come to him the way a birthday does, through the mail, requiring almost nothing of him except a decision.

He stood at the counter on a Saturday morning with a pen and a slice of toast he wasn't eating. His grandfather was at the table doing the crossword in pencil, which he claimed was not cheating but caution. Nicolas slid the envelope toward himself and then away again.

"Are you going to vote or just groom it," the old man said, not looking up.

"I'm deciding whether it matters." Nicolas had said some version of this to Louis-Thomas at school, and Louis-Thomas had shrugged and said one vote was a rounding error in a country of millions, which was the kind of thing Louis-Thomas said when he wanted to sound like he'd already given up. Karim had answered differently, something about how if none of them voted then nobody like them got counted at all, but that had felt less like an argument than like an appeal, and Nicolas didn't want to be appealed to. He wanted a reason that held weight in his own hand.

His grandfather put down the pencil. "You know where your vote came from?"

"The Constitution. Somewhere in there."

"The part for you. Eighteen." He tapped the table twice, as if marking a beat. "When they were trying to lower the voting age to eighteen, the supporters had a slogan. Old enough to fight, old enough to vote. Because eighteen-year-olds could be drafted for the Vietnam War."

Nicolas turned this over. He tried to picture the arithmetic of it: old enough that the state could send you, not old enough that you could send the state. It was a strange kind of proof, he thought, the sort that used your own body as the unit of measurement. Karim would like that framing. Louis-Thomas would say the draft was gone now and the argument with it, and Nicolas could already hear himself answering that the argument had never been about the draft itself, only about what counted as adult. He noticed, with some interest, that he was already composing both sides of a conversation that hadn't happened.

He looked at the ballot in its sealed envelope and wondered how his one mark connected to any of that. Whether a right earned by other people's danger transferred to someone whose greatest civic burden so far was jury duty paperwork and this pen. It didn't transfer, exactly. Nothing did. But it arrived, and it was addressed to him, and happenstance had put it in his hands on a morning when he had nothing better to do than be honest about what he believed.

"I still don't know if one vote matters," he said.

"Neither did they," his grandfather said. "They knew the draft mattered. The vote was the argument about what to do about it." He picked the pencil back up. "Six letters. Reluctant."

"Unwilling."

"That's nine."

Nicolas laughed, and something in him loosened. He understood now that his two friends weren't really opposed; they were looking at the same object from opposite ends, one seeing the futility of a single grain and the other seeing the size of the pile. He didn't have to choose an end. He could hold both and still mark the ballot. It was a strange comfort, uncertainty that didn't paralyze. He would vote without pretending the vote was more than it was, and refuse to skip it without pretending the skip was more than it was. His grandfather had sensitized him, he supposed, to the weight of the thing, though the old man would deny doing anything but a crossword.

He tore the envelope open. The instructions were in three languages, which struck him as its own small argument about who counted. He read the propositions, found the one about the school board funding he'd argued about with Karim on the bus, found the one Louis-Thomas's sardonic little brother called the tax thing, and marked his choices in blue ink, checking twice that it bled through nowhere.

He sealed it, put on his jacket, and walked the four blocks to the drop box outside the library, where a woman was taping a poster about election day hours. He fed the envelope into the slot and heard it land with a papery sound against the others.

"First time?" the woman asked.

Nicolas put his cold hands in his pockets. "Old enough," he said.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: A blind spot is an area around a car the driver cannot see from the seat, even with mirrors, which is why drivers turn their heads to check before changing lanes.
story:
Raphael had the key twisted in the ignition before Mr. Ahmadi finished clipping in his seatbelt, which was the first mistake of the afternoon, though neither of them counted it yet. The borrowed sedan belonged to Mr. Ahmadi's wife, and it smelled like her, like mint gum and hand lotion, which made Raphael feel he was borrowing something more than a car. The street outside was the kind of quiet suburban block where nothing moved except a sprinkler two houses down, sweeping its arc with the patience of a thing that had nowhere else to be.

"Mirror, signal, shoulder, then go," Mr. Ahmadi said. "In that order, every time." He was a neighbour, not a driving instructor, just a man with an afternoon free and a wife who trusted him with her obsolescent car, an old model with manual windows and a radio that only got one station clearly. He had told Raphael's mother he would take him out twice before the proper lessons began, as a favour, as something fathers did for each other's sons. Raphael's own father was in another province now, and the favour had a weight to it that Raphael didn't want to look at directly.

The car crawled down the street at fifteen miles an hour. Raphael held the wheel the way he held a controller, thumbs hooked, and Mr. Ahmadi said nothing about that either. They passed the house where Zane lived, and Raphael thought of Zane's older brother who had failed his test twice and joked about it at school, and of Sylas, who had passed first try and never mentioned it, which was somehow worse. All three of them were turning seventeen within months, and the licence had become a kind of currency among them, though none of them would admit it out loud.

At the end of the street the world opened onto a busier road, four lanes, traffic lights, a shopping plaza with an archipelago of parked carts stranded across the lot. "Right turn, then we'll get in the left lane at the second light," Mr. Ahmadi said. Raphael turned right, too widely, mounting half a wheel over the curb, and a driver behind them honked once, short and almost polite. His hands were sweating through the wheel's worn leather. He realized he had been so busy introspect about how he appeared from outside, what the honking driver thought of him, that he had stopped watching the road itself, and he filed that away as a thing to keep.

The second light came up. He signaled left, checked the side mirror, saw nothing, and began to drift the wheel. The horn that came then was nothing like polite. A grey hatchback sat beside them, close enough that Raphael could see the driver's startled face, a woman maybe thirty, one hand lifted off the wheel in that universal gesture of where did you come from. Mr. Ahmadi's arm was already across Raphael's chest, braced against the door, and the car had straightened itself before Raphael understood he had straightened it, some reflex older than his thinking.

"Pull in at the plaza," Mr. Ahmadi said, quiet.

They sat in a spot between two lines of faded paint, engine running, and Raphael's heart was going like he'd run the length of a field. "I checked the mirror," he said. "I checked it. She wasn't there."

"She was in his blind spot," Mr. Ahmadi said, nodding at the hatchback parked three spaces over, the woman now walking into the pharmacy as if nothing had happened. "An area around the car the driver can't see from the seat. Even with mirrors."

"So the mirror's useless."

"The mirror's fine. The seat is the problem." He tapped his own shoulder. "That's why you turn your head. Mirrors first, then look, then move."

Raphael turned his head now, experimentally, and saw the whole lane behind them open up, a stretch of asphalt the mirror had been quietly hiding all afternoon. It was strange to think of a gap like that, a hole in what he could know, sitting right beside him the whole time. He wanted to say something clever about it, tie it to something larger, and then decided not to. Zane would have made a joke. Sylas would have said nothing and driven on. Raphael sat somewhere between the two of them, as usual, and let the fact simply be a fact.

They did the loop again, back onto the busy road, and at the second light Raphael signaled, looked in the mirror, then turned his head and found a delivery van sitting exactly where the hatchback had been, patient and visible and waiting to be seen. He held the lane until it passed, then moved over clean. Mr. Ahmadi said nothing, which was its own kind of praise. They drove home through the quiet street at twenty miles an hour, the sprinkler still sweeping, and Raphael parked in front of his own house with only one small correction from the curb.

He sat with his hands still on the wheel while Mr. Ahmadi unclipped his belt. "I'm going to get it wrong again," Raphael said.

"Probably," Mr. Ahmadi agreed. He opened the door, then paused. "Same time Thursday?"

Raphael nodded, watched him walk up the driveway, and sat a moment longer, turning his head left, then right, taking in the whole street.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: A 2010 study claimed 'power poses' raised testosterone and lowered cortisol, but a larger 2015 replication found no such hormonal effect, though people still reported feeling more powerful.
story:
Rebecca had chosen the playground for practice because it was the only place where nobody asked questions. She sat on a swing that was too low for her now, her knees bent up near the handlebars, holding a printed page of interview questions against the wind. Abdullah arrived with two iced coffees and the unhurried look of someone who had already done this, because he had: hired last month at the garden center, first interview of his life.

"Question one," he said, settling onto the slide's ladder. "Tell me about yourself." Rebecca launched into an answer about being a responsible student, and he stopped her almost immediately. "You were looking at the wood chips."

"I was organizing my thoughts."

"You were hiding." He was not unkind about it. He made her do it again, and again, and on the fourth attempt she held his gaze for a full sentence before her eyes dropped to the mulch, where a pigeon was investigating a discarded fry. The pigeon, she thought, had better composure than she did.

That night Rosalie sent her a message, and Rebecca read it twice under her blanket: "Ok so don't mock this. Before my mom's interview she stood in the bathroom like Wonder Woman, hands on hips, for two minutes. There was this study, 2010, said power poses raise testosterone and lower cortisol. She swears it's why she got the job. Abdullah says don't predicate your whole confidence on one study, and honestly I don't know who's right. Try it and tell me. Also you owe me a swing date." Rebecca typed back that she would try anything once, including standing like a superhero in a public restroom, which was probably a misdemeanor.

She looked it up herself the next day in the library, because Rosalie's version felt too tidy, like a rule you could follow instead of a claim you could test. The 2010 study did exist, and it did say what Rosalie had said. But a larger replication in 2015 had found no such hormonal effect at all. What lingered was stranger and smaller: people who struck the poses still reported feeling more powerful. Rebecca sat with that for a while, watching the cursor blink. Nothing in her blood had necessarily changed, and yet something had, or people believed it had, and she could not decide whether the difference between those two things mattered. Maybe the feeling was the only part you could use anyway.

On the morning of the interview she stood in the coffee shop's restroom with her hands on her hips and her feet wide, feeling ridiculous, feeling, also, a slow warmth of certainty that she knew was not testosterone. It was more like a decision she was making in her body instead of her head. The 2015 study had not taken that away from her. It had only made her honest about what she was doing: choosing to feel powerful rather than being made powerful, an act of will she could not fully defend and did not need to.

The manager, a tired woman with a clipboard, asked why she wanted to work at a bakery. Rebecca kept her eyes up. She talked about early mornings, about the way bread smelled different from the street than from inside, about wanting to learn the register. One answer came out tangled and she said, "Let me try that again," and the woman waited, almost pleasantly, while she rebuilt it. Abdullah had been her first, unpolished audience, but the tangled-and-retried answer was hers alone, the thing she had practiced between the swings.

Walking out, she texted Rosalie from the corner by the swings: "Did the pose. Felt like a fraud for 10 seconds then just felt tall. No hormones were harmed. Will know by Friday." She pocketed the phone, pushed off from the fence, and crossed the playground toward the bus stop, chin level, looking at nothing in particular except straight ahead.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In England, a tenancy deposit is capped at five weeks' rent when the annual rent is under 50,000 pounds, and at six weeks' rent when it is 50,000 pounds or more.
story:
Maelie had thirty-one minutes before her driving lesson and two apartment leases on the table of the waiting room, which smelled of instant coffee and the ghost of a thousand nervous teenagers. Her mother had texted twice already: the letting agent wanted an answer by five o'clock, because someone else had viewed the flat on Hollow Lane and was "very keen." Very keen was estate agent for breathing, in Maelie's opinion, but still, five o'clock was five o'clock.

"Is that homework?" Edmond dropped into the chair beside her, holding two vending machine coffees, one of which he set in front of her like a tribute. "Because if you're doing homework in a driving school waiting room, that's the saddest thing I've seen all week, and yesterday I watched Kailey parallel park into a hedge."

"It's not homework. It's my flat." Maelie smoothed the pages out. One was for the flat on Hollow Lane, five hundred and twenty a month; the other was a studio near the river at four hundred and eighty, but with water rates and electricity on top, and a shorter notice period, and no washing machine. "For next year. In England. I have to work out which one actually costs less per month, everything included, and tell the agent by five."

Edmond leaned over the pages with the seriousness of a man inspecting a curry. "This one's cheaper."

"That one is cheaper the way a cat is a small tiger," said Maelie, and wrote 480 + 34 + 61 in the margin. "Then you add water, then you subtract the fact that the other one includes everything, then you add the fact that I'd have to take a bus to the laundrette, which is money and also a kind of suffering." She was still acclimating to the idea that a number on a poster and a number in your life were different numbers, and the gap between them was where all your cleverness was supposed to live.

Kailey arrived at a run, hair still damp from netball, and slid into the seat on Maelie's other side. "Am I late? Tell me I'm not late. Mr. Ndlovu gives me the look when I'm late."

"You are exactly on time," said Mr. Ndlovu himself, appearing in the doorway with the clipboard that functioned, in the economy of the driving school, as metonymy for his entire authority. The clipboard was him; he was, in a sense, the clipboard. "Three minutes, Maelie, then we are in the car. Theory first, then hill starts, and if you roll back on the hill I will pretend not to have seen it, once." He was not choleric by nature, but he had a register he used for lateness and rolled cars, and everyone respected it.

"Three minutes," Maelie repeated, and went back to the deposit lines, because there it was, the thing she'd been circling. The Hollow Lane landlord wanted a deposit of seven hundred and fifty, which felt vaguely like a lot, and she had a memory, half-digested from a forum at two in the morning, that there was a rule about this. She did the arithmetic on the back of the receipt from the vending machine. Five hundred and twenty a month was six thousand two hundred and forty a year, which was nowhere near fifty,000, so the deposit was capped at five weeks' rent. Five weeks of five hundred and twenty. Five hundred and twenty times five, divided by four, plus a bit. Six hundred and fifty. She checked it twice and then a third time, because the arithmetic was the easy part and the trusting of her own arithmetic was the hard part.

"Edmond," she said, "annual rent under fifty thousand pounds, deposit capped at five weeks. Fifty thousand or over, six weeks. That's the rule, right? That's what it said?"

"Sounds like the rule," said Edmond, who had no idea but had learned that confidence was socially useful.

"He's asking seven fifty," said Maelie. "That's a hundred pounds over. That's a hundred pounds of my money being requested in a way that is not allowed to be requested." She felt the two halves of her evening click together, the careful accountant and the person who actually had to live somewhere, and the position she arrived at was: studio by the river, total monthly with utilities six hundred and nineteen against Hollow Lane's six hundred and forty even before the laundrette, and a deposit that respected the cap, and she would say so, politely, in an email she would draft in the car park.

She emailed the agent from the pavement, then looked up. Mr. Ndlovu was standing by the little red hatchback with his arms folded, and the sun was doing something golden and unearned to the roof of it.

"Hill starts," he said. "Now. And Maelie, whatever you just calculated, I hope you calculated it better than you calculated your last three point turn."

"I'll have you know that three point turn was artistic," said Maelie, and got in on the driver's side.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Methane traps far more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide, but a methane molecule stays in the atmosphere for only about a decade on average, much less time than carbon dioxide.
story:
Colton spread the printout across the kitchen table and pinned the corner with a mug that had gone cold an hour ago. The graph showed a line climbing in small annual steps from roughly 280 parts per million to over 420, the last forty years steeper than the first, like a road that only remembers it is uphill once it is too steep to ignore. He had to explain it Monday, to Ms. Balogun's second-period class, and he had promised Theo they would figure it out together, though Theo was currently in the kitchen raiding the fridge as if studying were a sport with a halftime.

"I don't get why it's called trapping," Theo said, returning with cheese and crackers balanced on a plate. "The sun's heat comes in, and the gases keep it from leaving. So it's more like a lid."

"It's not a lid," Colton said. "A lid is solid. The gases let sunlight through, and then the heat that radiates back up off the ground, the infrared, some of it gets absorbed and re-emitted downward. The atmosphere isn't a blanket so much as a one-way door with a bouncer." He had read that somewhere, or something like it, and it had an embryonic feel to it still, the shape of an explanation without the weight.

Theo crunched. "So then just cut everything and we're fine."

"That's the part I keep getting wrong." Colton pulled up the notes he'd taken from a video the night before, a video he had watched twice because the first time he'd misunderstood it entirely. In middle school he had told a teacher, confidently and publicly, that methane was worse than carbon dioxide and that was that. Ms. Balogun had been standing nearby at some science fair or other, and he remembered her pause, the kind that let a wrong answer hang in the air long enough for the person who gave it to hear it themselves. He had never corrected the record. It had followed him in small ways, the way embarrassing things do, and now here was a chance to instantiate the fix, to put the real version into the world.

"Okay, so here's what I found," he said, turning the laptop toward Theo. "Methane traps far more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide. Way more. So you're right that it's stronger, pound for pound. But." He held up a finger. "A methane molecule stays in the atmosphere for only about a decade on average. Much less time than carbon dioxide. CO2 just sits there, basically for centuries."

Theo stopped chewing. "So if we plug the methane leaks tomorrow, the methane that's already up there mostly clears out in ten, twenty years, and warming slows faster in the near term. But if we only do methane and keep burning stuff, the CO2 keeps piling up forever."

"Right. And if we only do CO2, the methane we've already leaked keeps cooking us hard for the next decade even while we cut." Colton leaned back. "So which one would you do first, if you actually wanted to slow warming in the next few years?"

"Both," Theo said immediately.

"Both isn't an answer, that's a wish."

"Both is an answer when both is the answer." Theo pointed the cracker at the graph. "Look at that line. That's what happens when nobody's answer is both."

Colton looked. The line climbed its small stubborn steps, and he thought about how the argument they were having was the same one adults were having in rooms he would never see, except the adults got to vote on it. He didn't know yet how to weigh a strong gas that left quickly against a weaker one that never left; he only knew that the honest answer included both numbers and the time they lived in the sky, and that saying so out loud on Monday would mean admitting the middle-school version of himself had been confidently wrong. That admission still sat oddly in him, part relief, part dread.

He picked up the cold mug and moved it to the counter, then smoothed the graph flat where the paper had buckled. "Okay," he said. "New plan. I open with the line going up. Then I say: strong and short-lived versus weak and long-lived, and I don't pretend there's one lever."

Theo stacked his plate on the mug. "And if someone asks which to cut first?"

Colton looked at the steep last forty years of the line, then out the window where the streetlight had just come on, orange and steady against the dark. "Then I'll say it depends on how many years you're counting."

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Supercompensation is the idea that the body gets fitter during recovery after training, when it rebuilds beyond its previous level, not during the workout itself.
story:
Edouard had made the backyard into a kind of laboratory, though he would never have called it that. The fence marked his hundred metres, out to the compost bin and back, and every evening after dinner he ran it eight times while his father washed dishes behind the kitchen window and pretended not to watch. Edouard timed himself on his phone, which lay in the grass beside the hose reel, and he kept the times in a note titled simply PROGRAM. The times were getting worse. That was the problem. Two weeks ago he had run the fourth sprint in 13.6; last night the fourth had taken him 14.9, and the sixth 15.4, and he had stopped before the eighth, standing with his hands on his knees near the rhododendron while the sprinkler ticked over somewhere behind the garage.

Pyper came over on Saturday with a bag of apricots from her tree and sat on the overturned wheelbarrow to watch him do his sprints. She had run club track in the winter and quit in the spring for reasons she described, when pressed, as administrative. She counted his reps out loud in a flat voice, and when he finished the sixth and lay down on the dry patch of grass by the fence, she said, "You do this every day?" He said he did, obviously, that was the whole point of a program. She peeled an apricot and said nothing, which he found more irritating than if she had argued.

"It's called supercompensation," she said eventually, still looking at the apricot. "I'm not explaining it. Look it up or don't."

He looked it up, that night, sitting on the back step with the porch light attracting moths. The body gets fitter during recovery, not during the workout itself; after training, during rest, it rebuilds beyond its previous level. He read the sentence three times. It was one of those ideas that seemed, once you had it, so obvious that you felt slightly humiliated. All those evenings sprinting into the dusk, and the getting-fitter part had been happening, if it was happening at all, on the days he refused to take. He had been treating rest as a moral failure, a small pathologized weakness, rather than as the part of training where the actual work got done.

On Sunday he did not run. This turned out to be harder than running. By four o'clock a specific ennui had settled over the backyard, and he found himself walking the fence line anyway, counting his strides, until he caught himself and went inside to get paper. If rest was part of the program, then the program had to be written, had to be planned like anything else that mattered. He drew a grid on the back of a water bill: seven days, and across the top, sprint work, easy running, rest, warm-up. He filled in Monday and Tuesday before he stopped, because Wednesday through Sunday resisted him. How much rest was enough? How would he know? He sat with the pen until the light went.

Dillon found him at lunch on Monday sketching grids on his binder and diagnosed the problem in about six seconds. "You're planning your whole week in advance," Dillon said. "That's not a program, that's a prophecy." Dillon believed, on principle, in deciding everything the morning of, on the grounds that plans were for people who didn't trust themselves. They had argued about this for years, in the desultory way of people who argue partly for company. But now Edouard had something at stake. He said a program with rest days built in was exactly the kind of thing you couldn't improvise, because on the morning of a rest day you always felt like training, and on the morning of a hard day you always felt like resting. Dillon said that was his point. Edouard said that was the opposite of his point.

What he settled on, after two days of the argument running quietly under everything else he did, was a hybrid, and he was honest with himself that it was a compromise rather than a discovery. The week was written: warm-up and sprint work on Monday, easy running Tuesday, rest Wednesday, sprint work Thursday, rest Friday, a longer session Saturday, rest Sunday. But at the top of the page he added a line he'd thought of while dragging the hose across the grass: times decide. If Monday's numbers were worse than the week before, the week got easier, and if they were better, it stayed. The plan gave the week its shape; the times told him whether the shape was right. He did not know yet whether that would work. He wrote it in pencil.

The warm-up he learned from a video, and it embarrassed him, so he did it at six in the morning before anyone was awake: leg swings holding the fence, high knees across the lawn, slow skips past the compost bin where the neighbour's cat watched him with flat suspicion. Mr. Perera, who was always up early spraying his roses on the other side of the fence, watched one morning and said, "In my day we just ran." Edouard said that was probably why everyone's knees were terrible, and Mr. Perera laughed in a way that suggested he had been hoping to be argued with.

The first Wednesday rest day was still bad. The second one was less bad. On the second Monday, the fourth sprint came in at 13.8, and on the Monday after that, 13.4, which was faster than anything from his every-day weeks. He stood over the phone in the grass for a while, letting that settle. He was aware that he could not entirely trust the number, that days had moods the way people did, that two good Mondays were not a seismic shift in anything except his own willingness to keep going. He was aware that he still didn't know where the line was, how much rest turned from enough into too much, and that the only way to find out was to cross it and get slower again and adjust.

Dillon came by on Saturday to see the fence course. Edouard showed him the water-bill grid with its pencilled line at the top, times decide, and Dillon read it twice and said, grudgingly, "So the plan is a draft and the stopwatch is the editor." Edouard said that was exactly it, and that he wished he'd said it that way. Pyper, who had arrived somewhere in the middle of this and was eating apricots on the wheelbarrow again, asked what Thursday looked like, because Thursdays were free.

Edouard took out the pencil. The sprinkler came on by the garage, ticking its slow arc across the corner of the lawn, and he stood in the last of the light holding the grid against the fence, and wrote Thursday's name in beside hers.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In Arthur Aron's 1997 study, pairs of strangers took turns asking each other 36 questions that grew gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk.
story:
Natalie had read the message so many times that afternoon that the words had stopped looking like words. "coffee at the kiosk in ridgeway park, saturday, 2?" That was all, followed by the boy's name at the top of the thread, though she had long since stopped needing to see it. She had typed and deleted three replies, and finally she sent the fourth to Hafsa instead: "he asked me. park. saturday. what do i even do with my hands."

Hafsa's answer came back in a burst: "you have HANDS??? since WHEN" and then, a minute later, a second message, more serious. "just talk to him like he's a person and not a test you have to pass. also don't wear the shoes you can't walk in. the park is gravel." Natalie read it twice, holding the phone against her chest between readings, as if the advice might evaporate. It was good advice. It was also, she suspected, the kind of advice that only worked for people who did not already know, with total certainty, that they were being tested.

She arrived twelve minutes early, which she had planned, so that she could be the one already sitting down, already comfortable, already belonging to the bench the way a person with nothing to prove would belong to it. The kiosk stood at the edge of the park where the mown grass gave way to a steeper trail, and above the treeline the hills rose in pale, scrubby tiers. A montane haze hung over the ridges, that thin bluish blur that made far things look softer than near things, and Natalie thought, with some resentment, that it was very beautiful, that it was showing off, that it was making her nerves look ridiculous by comparison.

He showed up on time, in a shirt she had never seen, which was somehow startling, the way a teacher is startling in a supermarket. They bought coffees. They sat. And then the conversation, which had flowed so easily through a screen for three weeks, ran out the way water runs out of a cracked cup. They covered the weather. They covered the coffee. They covered the fact that the coffee was hot. She watched his eyes drift once toward the trail, and she understood that he was calculating whether leaving was yet socially possible, and the fear coagulated in her chest, thick and specific, a fear with edges.

"Okay," she said, before she could stop herself. "I read about this thing. There was a study in 1997, by a guy named Arthur Aron. Pairs of strangers took turns asking each other thirty-six questions, and they got more and more personal as they went. And after, those pairs felt closer than pairs who just made small talk." She heard how it sounded, like she was proposing a lab experiment, and her face went hot. "It's not a test. I mean, it is, technically, it's a study, but we don't have to. Forget it."

He was quiet for a second, turning his cup on its saucer, and she braced for the polite retreat. "What kind of questions," he said. "Like math?"

"Like, the first ones aren't much. What would constitute a perfect day for you. Stuff like that. Then they get harder."

"Harder how?"

"Harder like, tell your partner something you like about them already. And later it's stuff about your family and what you're afraid of." She shrugged, aiming for casual and landing somewhere near it. "Nobody's making us. But the small talk isn't working, and I'd rather fail at something interesting than succeed at talking about coffee."

A slow smile, mostly at one corner of his mouth. "A perfect day for me," he said, "is raining, and I'm inside, and there's a football match on that nobody else in my house cares about, so no one talks to me for two hours." And that was it, that was question one, answered without ceremony, and Natalie found that her hands had stopped being a problem because they were busy holding her cup.

They did not do all thirty-six. By question eight they had wandered off the list entirely, and by question twelve the list was a distant ancestor of whatever conversation they were actually having, one that looped and doubled back and occasionally went quiet in a way that no longer frightened her. He told her about his grandmother's house being sold. She told him about the year her parents' marriage had quietly achieved homeostasis, a word she used and then had to explain, a steady state where nothing got worse and nothing got better and everyone called it fine. He said that was the saddest definition of fine he'd ever heard. Nobody had ever said anything that accurate to her before.

Mr. Almeida, who taught chemistry at their school and apparently spent Saturdays power-walking the park's loop, passed them twice. The second time he slowed, took in the two of them leaning toward each other over the kiosk's wobbly table, and raised his eyebrows at Natalie with an expression she chose to interpret as benevolent. "Don't let me interrupt the summit," he said, and kept walking, and the boy laughed, and she laughed, and it was fine, actually fine, the real kind.

The light was going amber when they finally stood, and the montane ridges had gone from blue to violet. She had not asked him any of the last questions, the ones near the end of the list, the ones about love and sharing everything. She didn't know yet whether the study meant anything outside a study, whether thirty-six questions made closeness or whether the kind of person willing to ask them was already halfway there. Both could be true. She held that thought the way she held the cooling cup, without needing to resolve it.

"So," he said, hands in his pockets, gravel crunching under his shifting weight. "That was, what, twelve?"

"Fourteen. I counted."

"Twenty-two to go." He looked at the trailhead, then back at her. "Same time next Saturday?"

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Caramelization is the browning of sugar on its own, without proteins; table sugar begins to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius.
story:
Aidan set the heavy pot on the stove before his mother's car had fully left the driveway, because tonight was his turn and tonight, for once, he intended to be ready. The chicken was braising in the oven, the rice was measured, and on the counter beside the stove sat a bag of sugar, a pat of butter, and a small carton of cream. Caramel sauce for over the sliced apples. He had promised Kirsten at school that he would attempt it, and Kirsten had looked at him with that flat, noncommittal expression she saved for announcements she considered doomed.

"You'll burn it," she had said. "Everyone burns the first one."

He had ascribed her doubt to sour grapes, since Kirsten herself had ruined a batch of brownies at the chemistry club bake sale and never quite recovered from the humiliation. But standing alone in the kitchen now, watching the sugar heap in the pan, he could not entirely dismiss her. His father's phone call from the hospital cafeteria came back to him, unbidden. Two springs ago, before the surgery, his father had stood in this same kitchen and made caramel in this same pan, and Aidan had watched from the doorway, too afraid of the hot sugar and too afraid of the man to come closer. "See how it goes clear first," his father had said then, tilting the pan without looking up. "Then it turns. You wait for the turn." Aidan had never asked what the turn was, exactly, because his father's patience that evening had felt like something borrowed, something that had to be returned.

He turned the burner to medium and added a splash of water to the sugar, the way the recipe on his phone described. The crystals hissed, dissolved, went glassy. He stood very still. The phone said to wash down the sides of the pan with a wet pastry brush, and he did, twice, frowning at the pan like it might betray him.

The mixture stayed pale. He waited. It stayed pale. He turned the heat up a notch, and the syrup began to bubble in slow, thick rings, and still it sat there, stubbornly colorless, and he began to wonder whether his father had performed some trick he had not shown. Somewhere outside a car door slammed, and he flinched, and the syrup flared suddenly amber at the edges, spreading inward like a rumor.

"Whoa," he said out loud, to nobody.

He reached for the handle and then pulled his hand back. Too early, the sauce would be thin and too sweet; too late, it would taste of ash and he would have to throw it out and start over with the clock running down, his mother due home in forty minutes with his little brother, who would announce the failure at the table with the tact of a seven-year-old. He grabbed his phone and typed fast with one thumb: caramel question. The first result said table sugar begins to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius. He read it twice. A hundred and seventy. He had no thermometer.

What he did have was memory. His father had never used a thermometer either. His father had watched, the way sailors used to watch the sky, and Aidan understood, with a small cold shock, that watching was not the same as guessing. The color was the measurement. He needed the amber to deepen to something like old copper, the color of the syrup in his memory, and then it would be ready, and everything before that was patience.

Mr. Rossi's voice drifted through the window from the next yard, arguing cheerfully with someone about a soccer match, and Aidan found the ordinary sound steadying. He watched the pan. The amber deepened. At copper, still not quite, the edges threatening to slide toward red, he made the call, pulled the pan off the heat, and dropped in the butter. It seized and spat. He poured the cream in a thin stream, whisking hard, and the sauce roared up and then settled into something glossy and dark gold that smelled like the kitchen had smelled two springs ago, before everything.

He dipped a spoon, blew on it, tasted. Smooth, faintly bitter at the finish, which the recipe claimed was correct. He tasted again to be sure and decided the recipe could be ascribed some small authority, at least for tonight.

The front door opened while he was pouring the sauce into a jar. His mother came in with grocery bags, his brother behind her, and she stopped in the doorway of the kitchen and looked at the braising chicken, the rice steaming under a lid, the jar of caramel catching the overhead light.

"Who taught you that?" she said.

"A guy at school," Aidan said.

She set the bags down slowly. "You mean your dad," she said.

"I mean I figured it out." He tightened the jar lid. He wanted to say more, something about the pan and the color and the phone call he had not returned last week when his father asked about the game, but the sentence would not assemble itself honestly. He had used his father's trick and pretended it was his own acumen, and both things were true at once, and neither cancelled the other.

At dinner his brother demanded the caramel on everything, including the rice, and their mother allowed it once, and Aidan watched the sauce pour in a dark ribbon and thought about texting his father a picture of the jar. His phone sat face down beside his plate. He turned it over, then over again, and left it where it was.

"Next time," his brother said, mouth full, "make more."

"There's plenty," Aidan said, and got up to get the jar, and found it already empty, licked clean, standing rinsed and upside down on the drying rack like it had never held anything at all.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: A dot after a note adds half the note's value, so a dotted half note lasts three beats in 4/4 time.
story:
The community centre smelled of chlorine from the pool down the hall and old coffee from the vending machine nobody had cleaned since spring, and in the small room off the gym, behind a folding partition, Mason sat with a keyboard, a pencil, and sixteen empty staves drawn on photocopied paper. Mr. Reddy had assigned it on Tuesday: a melody of sixteen bars, with chord changes, written properly in standard notation by Friday. "Not recorded," he had said. "Not hummed at me. Written."

Mason had been playing guitar by ear since he was nine, and he had never once written anything down. The melody lived in his hands, in the calluses, in the particular way his thumb picked the low string while his fingers found a shape that had no name he knew. When he tried to circumscribe it on paper, to trap it in note heads and stems and bar lines, it thinned out. The third bar was the problem. He tapped the keyboard key for the long F he wanted, held it, counted, and came up short.

Karsen was at the next table copying someone's chemistry homework, or pretending to; Keith had his feet up on a chair, watching. "It's out of sync," Karsen said without looking up. "You sing it right and then you play it wrong."

"I hold the note longer than I'm writing it," Mason said. He had written a half note, two beats, in a bar of four, and then two quarter notes, and the bar still needed something it wasn't getting. He tapped his pencil against the music stand. The room's radiator clanked, and somewhere down the corridor a basketball game's shoes squeaked in bursts.

Keith wandered over and squinted at the page. "Why's that bar look emptier than the others?"

"Because I'm a beat short. In 4/4, every bar has four beats, and mine has three." Mason played what he'd written. It was true. The melody wanted to lean into that F and wait, and the paper let it wait only two beats, and then everything after arrived too early, like a conversation where he kept interrupting himself.

He thought of his grandfather, who had played wedding music in a village church and never learned notation at all, everything autochthonous to his fingers, grown from the place and nowhere else, songs nobody could recover now that he was gone. Mason had asked him once why he never wrote the songs down, and his grandfather had said, "They're not for paper." At the time it had sounded wise. Now it sounded like a door closing.

Mr. Reddy came in with a thermos and a stack of sheet music, sat at the far keyboard, and played a scale quietly, not looking at anyone. Mason got up anyway, carried the page over, and pointed at the third bar. "How do I make a note last longer without changing the rhythm after it?"

Mr. Reddy took his glasses off, looked at the bar, and handed the page back. "Count what you sing," he said, and went back to his scale. That was all. Mason stood there a moment, then walked back with the page warm in his hand.

He sang the third bar into the chlorine-smelling air, slow, the way it wanted to go, and tapped his foot, and his foot came down one, two, three before the melody moved on. Three beats. Not two. In his head the note was three beats long and the bar needed four beats' worth and it already had one beat of something after the F. He erased the half note and stared at where it had been. A whole note was too much. Two quarter notes were wrong. He needed something between.

Karsen leaned over from the next table. "What's that little dot on the tune Mr. Reddy left on the piano?"

Mason walked to the upright piano against the wall where somebody's abandoned exercise book lay open, and there it was, a half note with a small dot after it, sitting alone in a bar. He counted the bar under his breath. Four beats, and the dotted note filled three of them. He tried it in his own bar: a half note, a dot after it, and one quarter note. Three and one. He counted. Four.

He drew the dot onto his own page with a hand not quite steady, sat at the keyboard, and played the third bar through. The F leaned and waited, three whole beats, and then the melody stepped onward, and for the first time the paper sounded like his hands. It cost him something he couldn't name, though. The song, caught in ink, was now a thing anyone could play, and it belonged a little less to him.

Keith clapped twice, lazily. Karsen said, "Finally," and went back to the chemistry.

Mason looked down the remaining twelve bars, most of them still blank, the pencil sharpened beside his wrist. He pressed the F key once more, softly, listening to it decay.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: For the same sample size, a poll's margin of error is largest when opinion is split near 50 percent, and pollsters usually report that largest figure.
story:
Antoine had claimed the folding table outside the gymnasium doors at six in the morning, before the poll workers had even finished taping the arrows to the floor. By seven he had his clipboard, his tally sheet, and a sign that read EXIT POLL, SCHOOL PROJECT, PLEASE STOP, and by seven fifteen he had learned that exactly nobody wanted to stop on their way to vote in the most important municipal election of their lifetimes. The school paper needed his numbers by six, print deadline, no exceptions, and he had promised the editor a prediction for the mayor's race and a prediction for the school board question that shared the ballot.

He was seventeen, which meant he could not vote himself, a fact his mother had called "good practice for disappointment" over breakfast. He could, however, stand four metres from the door with Dayne and Mina, both of whom had agreed to help in exchange of a promise he now regretted, that he would stop saying the word "methodology" before noon.

"Forty-two respondents," he announced at ten, as though reading a score. "Hargrove twenty-four, Okafor eighteen." Mina was logging answers on her phone. Dayne was eating a granola bar he had found in Mina's bag, which she described as "an externality of your presence, Dayne, the costs you impose on everyone around you," and Dayne had laughed so hard a voter stopped to see what was happening and ended up taking the survey, which Antoine counted as data collection by charm.

The problem surfaced at noon, over the sandwiches Mina had brought because Dayne had eaten everything else. Antoine's sheet had two races. The mayor's race was split nearly down the middle, twenty-four to eighteen with a handful undecided. The school board question, though, was a landslide: of the forty-two people, only one supported it. And yet when Antoine calculated his margin of error, he had written the same plus-or-minus figure next to both, because that was the number the website gave him for a sample of forty-two. It looked wrong. It sat on the page looking wrong.

"Text your brother," Mina said. "He does this for a living." Antoine's brother was a junior statistician in another city who answered messages the way other people answered prayers, eventually and with conditions. Antoine typed it out: two questions, one sample, one near unanimous, one near tie, same error number on both, am I doing something backwards? He pressed send and they all watched the phone as though it might transmute into an answer on its own. Dayne suggested, helpfully, that the margin of error might simply be "a number websites make up to seem humble."

The reply came at two, while a man in a runoff T-shirt was arguing with a poll worker about where the line started. Antoine read it aloud on the curb behind the table. His brother wrote that he wasn't backwards at all, that with the same sample size the margin of error is largest when opinion splits near fifty percent, and that pollsters usually report that largest figure, the worst case, so a lopsided question was actually more solid than the number suggested. So Hargrove's lead over Okafor was shakier than it looked, Antoine said slowly, and the school board blowout was more certain than it looked, and he had been treating them as equally doubtful because the reported number was the cautious one. Mina said, "So your tie race is where the error does its worst work," and Antoine nodded and felt something rearrange behind his forehead, two separate pictures clicking into one.

At five thirty he had sixty-one respondents, and the mayor's race was still inside the noise, and he had a choice. He could write the confident piece, HARGROVE BY SIX, and be right or wrong in public tomorrow, or he could write the honest piece, that his poll could not separate the candidates, that anyone claiming otherwise from a number like his was selling certainty nobody had. Dayne voted for the confident piece on the grounds that "the hedonistic seniors at this school only read headlines anyway." Mina voted for the honest piece and then, when Antoine kept staring at his tally sheet, said, "Antoine. Write the true one. You'll get to be smug either way by Thursday."

He filed at five fifty, ten minutes before the polls closed, and the last paragraph said the school board question would lose and he would stand behind that, while the mayor's race was, from his data, a coin he had not flipped enough times. Then the three of them sat on the curb with the last sandwiches and watched the doors, where a poll worker was carrying out the machine that would count everything properly, or at least count all of it, and Dayne raised his water bottle and said, "To methodology," and they all drank to that.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In the UK, a driver who passes the test in an automatic car may drive only automatic cars, and must pass a manual test to drive a manual car.
story:
The parking lot behind the shuttered garden centre had been chosen, the email said, for its generous margins. Rebecca read this in the passenger seat of Ms. Ito's little silver car while the instructor filled out a form on a clipboard, and she understood "generous margins" to mean that nobody expected her to be good at this.

"Right," said Ms. Ito. "Seat, mirror, seatbelt, and we'll see what you're made of." She said it the way people say things they say forty times a week. Rebecca adjusted the seat until her feet reached the pedals with a certain authority, checked the mirror in which she could see mostly sky, and fastened the belt. The gear lever between the seats had no numbers on it, only odd raised lines and letters, and it occurred to her, slowly, that she had never once seen her mother's car do anything with its own gears. Her mother's car, the one she was supposed to learn on eventually, had a lever you moved yourself, and a third pedal, and her mother had warned her about it in the tone reserved for family inheritances: you'll want to learn properly, or the car's no use to you.

She got the car moving. It lurched, stopped, lurched again, and then travelled a full fifteen metres at the speed of a slow bicycle, which felt, in the moment, like a personal triumph. The empty lot spread out around them, white lines fading into tarmac, one shopping trolley abandoned near a drain. Ms. Ito made a note on her clipboard. "Good. Again."

After the third circuit of the lampposts, a boy on a bike appeared at the lot's edge, cutting across on his way somewhere better. It was Kyan from school, who recognised the car, or her, and stood straddling the bike with one foot down, watching her do an eight-point turn around a painted bay. "Automatic lessons?" he called, when she wound the window down, which took her three tries because the button was on the driver's side and her hand kept going to the middle of the door.

"Obviously," Rebecca said. "You've seen me walk up stairs."

"Jacey's doing manual," he said. "She says it's grim now but worth it. Because if you pass in an automatic, that's all you can drive, automatics. You'd have to do another whole test to drive a manual." He said this with the mild cruelty of someone reporting weather. "And your mum's car's a manual, isn't it."

Ms. Ito, from the passenger seat, did not intervene, which Rebecca understood as its own kind of comment. She let the car roll forward a metre and braked, thinking. The lot was quiet enough that she could hear the tick of the indicator, which she had not meant to turn on. Kyan was still there, balanced on his bike, waiting for her to be annoyed, and she declined the invitation. "Thanks," she said. "Extremely germane." He grinned and pedalled off toward the retail park.

She drove another circuit, and her mind divided itself into two people, both reasonable. One observed that six fewer things to manage was not laziness, it was sense; that she could actually learn steering and judgement and mirrors without the morass of a clutch, and that the country was full of automatic cars now anyway. The other observed that her mother's car sat in the drive like a promise, that a second test meant twice the money and twice the examinations, and that doing the hard version first bought her everything the easy version bought, plus the lever and the third pedal. Neither person could prove the other stupid. She suspected that people who claimed to be certain about things like this had simply stopped listening to one side.

"There's a junction between now and then," said Ms. Ito, in the tone of someone who had watched a great deal of thinking happen behind the wheel. "Shall we try changing direction?"

They did. It was a wide, sweeping reverse around an island of cracked paint, and it went wrong twice and then, on the third attempt, surprisingly right, the car swinging clean in an arc that seemed, for two seconds, to belong to somebody competent. Something in her chest lifted, a small invigorating flare she would not have admitted to out loud.

She brought the car back to the start, set the brake, and sat with her hands still on the wheel. "Ms. Ito," she said. "If I called the office, could I switch the rest of my hours to manual?"

Ms. Ito wrote something on the clipboard and did not look up. "People do," she said. "Usually in week two, mind."

"I'm early," said Rebecca.

The instructor opened the driver's door and got out, unclipping the bright red L magnets from the boot. She held one out flat in her palm, warm from the sun. "Same time Thursday," she said. "Wear flat shoes. Your mother's car has a clutch, and you'll want to feel it."

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A counterfactual conditional describes what would have been true if things had been different, such as 'if Sally owned a donkey, she would ride it', and usually implies the 'if' part is false.
story:
Savannah arrived at seminar four minutes late with her essay still warm from the printer, folded twice in her back pocket. Ms. Chen had already arranged the desks in a horseshoe, and the only open seat was between Emy and the window, which meant everyone watched her cross the room. She sat down, unfolded the essay, and heard Ms. Chen say the thing she had been dreading: they would go around the circle, and each of them would defend one claim from their writing out loud.

"I can't," Emy whispered beside her. Emy had written hers in one sitting at two in the morning and wanted, more than anything, to get through the period without being asked to stand behind a single sentence. Savannah wanted the opposite. She had rewritten her conclusion three times, and what she wanted was to be challenged on it, because she wasn't sure it held.

Arya went first, as usual, with the confidence of someone who had never once wondered whether she was wrong. "If schools started an hour later, student performance would improve," Arya said. "The evidence is overwhelming."

"That's a conditional," Savannah said before she could stop herself.

Arya turned. "Obviously."

"No, I mean." Savannah looked down at her own paper, where she had circled a sentence in red. "My brother missed his bus on Tuesday and spent the whole ride in the car telling me that if he'd left five minutes earlier, he would have caught it. And he'd still be saying it now if I hadn't told him he can never check it. He can't go back and leave earlier. There's no world where he does." She paused. "Ms. Chen called it a counterfactual conditional last week. The 'if' part is false, and you're saying what would have been true if things had been different. Like, if Sally owned a donkey, she would ride it. Sally doesn't own a donkey."

Arya's mouth opened, then closed. "So my claim is what, worthless?"

"No. Yours is different." Savannah turned her essay over, then back again, because she was thinking faster than she could write. "Yours is testable. Schools could actually start later. You could run it. You could check it. My brother can't check his, ever, and that's not a small difference, that's the whole difference." The classroom smelled like whiteboard marker and the radiator's dry heat, and outside the window a groundskeeper was dragging a hose across the frost, and she made herself keep going. "But here's what I can't figure out. My whole conclusion is built on the untestable kind. I wrote that if the town had never built the bypass, the river district would still have its shops. I imputed a whole economy to a road that was never going to exist. I gave it effects. And I can't check any of it."

"Then why did you write it like a fact?" Arya said. It wasn't cruel, exactly. It was clipped, the way Arya asked everything.

"Because it read better," Savannah said, and heard how bad that sounded, and said it anyway. "Because 'this probably would have happened' is a weaker sentence."

"Emy," Ms. Chen said quietly, and Emy straightened like she'd been caught sleeping.

Emy looked at her paper for a long moment. "I wrote that if my grandmother had stayed in her village, she would have been happier." She said it fast, eyes still down. "I don't know if that's a fact. I don't think it's checkable either. I think I just wanted it to be true."

Nobody laughed. Arya was quiet for once, turning her pen over in her fingers, and Savannah understood that Arya's wish, all year, had been to be unarguable, and that the wish and the seminar were at odds, and that Arya was maybe figuring that out at the same moment Savannah was.

"Can I change my conclusion?" Savannah asked Ms. Chen. "Not to something safer. To something honest. I want to say that some claims are checkable and some aren't, and that knowing which is which is worth more than being sure."

Ms. Chen said the revision was due Thursday. Arya raised her hand and asked whether a prediction about the future counted as checkable, and the discussion moved on without resolving, and Savannah could feel it going on underneath the words like something subterranean, the whole class circling a question nobody would finish today.

After the bell, Emy caught her at the door. "Your brother," Emy said. "Did he leave five minutes earlier the next day?"

Savannah pulled her coat on. "He left ten. He caught it, and he said that proved him right."

"Proved what?"

Savannah shouldered her bag. "That's what I'm going to write about."

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: In Islamic law, ijtihad is the independent reasoning a qualified scholar uses to apply the Quran and hadith to questions the texts do not directly answer.
story:
The folding chairs at the community hall had been arranged in a horseshoe for Violet's cousin's aqiqah, and by the time the plates of biryani came out, the adults had colonized all of them, so Violet and Myla sat on the stage steps with their plates balanced on their knees. It was Myla who started it, in the way she started things, quietly and then all at once.

"Alexis asked me yesterday how scholars even rule on this stuff," Myla said. "Like, her dad does all his banking on his phone. Interest, loans, the whole thing. She said, the Quran's like fourteen hundred years old, right? Nobody had an app." She picked a cashew out of her rice and ate it separately, the way she always did. "I didn't know what to tell her."

Violet set her plate down. "There's a word for it," she said. "I read it somewhere. Ijtihad. It's the independent reasoning a qualified scholar uses to apply the Quran and hadith to questions the texts don't directly answer."

Myla looked at her. "You read that somewhere and just kept it in your pocket?"

Violet's uncle, two chairs away, turned around. "Who's talking about ijtihad at a party?"

"She is," Myla said, pointing with her fork.

"Then she should talk to Mr. Liu's son-in-law," the uncle said, and went back to his conversation about parking.

The son-in-law turned out to be a thin man in a grey kurta whom Violet had previously only seen holding somebody's baby. He was standing near the tea urn, and when Violet approached him he poured her a cup without being asked, which she took as permission. She laid out Alexis's question, the phone banking, the interest, the texts that could not have mentioned any of it, and waited.

"So people think it's either everything still applies or none of it does," he said. "As if the rule is vestigial, like an appendix, and modern life just cuts it out. But that's not how the tradition sees itself. There's reasoning, there's method. It's not guessing. And it's not prognosticating about the future either; it's working from the texts on the question in front of you." He stirred his tea. "A dissident with a website and a scholar doing ijtihad can sound identical to someone who hasn't read either one. The difference is training and the method, not just the conclusion."

Violet wrote ijtihad on the back of her hand with a pen from her jacket, because she knew herself well enough to know she would lose the word otherwise. "But who decides if someone's qualified?" she asked. "That's the part Alexis will ask next."

"That's the part we argue about," he said, and smiled into his cup. "Somebody's gatekeeping, always. Go argue with your friend. It's good practice."

On Monday, at the picnic table behind the school where the debate team ate when the cafeteria was too loud, Violet laid it out for Alexis and Myla both. She had printed two pages of notes, one from a comparative religion site and one from a page of translated hadith that Mr. Liu, who coached the team and kept a shelf of reference books in his van, had found for her. "So here's my position," she said. "The motion is whether ancient religious rules still apply to modern life, and I'm going to argue that the question is badly framed. The rule isn't the text sitting frozen. The rule is the reasoning, and the reasoning carries forward. That's ijtihad. It's what a qualified scholar uses to apply the Quran and hadith to questions the texts don't directly answer, like your dad's phone banking."

Alexis leaned across the table. "So who counts as qualified?"

"That's where it gets shaky," Violet said. "I can defend the method. I can't fully defend the gatekeeping, because different schools disagree about it and I don't read Arabic, so I'm taking everyone's word for the translations. I'll concede that in the rebuttal instead of pretending it's solid."

Mr. Liu, unwrapping a sandwich at the end of the table, raised his cup of instant noodles in her direction. "Conceding the right weakness is a skill," he said. "Most people concede the wrong one."

At the tournament on Saturday, the opponent, a boy in a blazer from the school across town, called religious law "a fixed document stretched over a changing world like old fabric." Violet stood at the podium with her notes on the ijtihad line and her conceded weakness printed at the bottom in small type, and heard Myla, in the second row, crack her knuckles the way she did before anything that mattered.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Kintsugi is a Japanese technique of repairing broken pottery with lacquer mixed or dusted with powdered gold, treating the break as part of the object's history rather than hiding it.
story:
The bowl broke at four in the afternoon, in her grandmother's kitchen, under a slant of light that had been sliding across the linoleum all day. Anna had been reaching for the sugar jar and her elbow caught the rim of the bowl where it sat drying on the rack, and it went over the edge in what felt like slow motion, striking the counter first and then the floor, splitting into three pieces with a small clean sound, like a knuckle cracking. She stood over it without moving. The bowl was older than her mother. It had come from Japan in her grandmother's suitcase in 1968, blue with a heron inside the bottom, and it was the one object in the house her grandmother would have rescued from a fire.

She gathered the pieces into her palms. The edges were sharp enough to be careful with, and one fragment held most of the heron's wing. Her first thought was glue, the yellow tube in the drawer by the stove, and she even got it out before she understood what she was doing: hiding it. Setting the seam so finely that in a year her grandmother would have forgotten there had ever been a break, and would run her thumb over a hairline ridge and wonder, and say nothing. Anna put the glue back. Something about that felt worse than the breaking.

Her grandmother was at Mr. Marino's, across the fence, arguing about his tomato stakes, which gave Anna maybe an hour. She sat on the kitchen floor with the pieces laid out on a dish towel and called Carina, who was the kind of person who knew things or knew where things were. "Kintsugi," Carina said, after Anna had described the bowl and the break and the feeling in her stomach. "It's a Japanese technique of repairing broken pottery with lacquer mixed or dusted with powdered gold. You leave the crack visible. On purpose."

"On purpose," Anna repeated.

"That's the whole point. The break becomes part of its history instead of something you hide. Look it up, I might be misremembering the details." Carina was not often wrong, but Anna looked it up anyway, kneeling by the router with her phone, and there it was: the same words, and photographs of bowls and cups veined with gold, the repairs unmistakable, almost proud. Anna had expected to feel relieved, and instead she felt the problem get heavier. It was one thing to fix a bowl. It was another to fix it in a way that announced the fix forever.

There was no lacquer in the house and no powdered gold, and the hardware store in town was closed on Sundays. She biked to the craft shop anyway, half hoping it would be closed too, so the decision would be made for her. It was open.
