The cashier, a woman with metamorphic-looking gray streaks in her black hair, found her a two-part epoxy and a tiny plastic vial of gold mica powder, and said the powder would never look like real gold, and Anna said she knew, and bought them both. On the ride back she invented, without wanting to, the conversation in which she confessed, and in every version her grandmother's face did something complicated that Anna could not read.

Back in the kitchen she mixed the epoxy on a paper plate and worked the first seam with a toothpick, pressing the pieces together until they held. Her hands were steady, which surprised her, because the rest of her was not. She had read enough to know that a person could not un-break a bowl, could only decide what the breaking meant. It occurred to her that she was choosing this not only for the bowl but to assuage her own guilt, and that the two motives were braided together in a way she couldn't separate, and she kept going anyway, dusting the wet seam with gold before the epoxy could skin over. The powder caught the afternoon light and glowed. It looked, she thought, like the bowl had a new vein of something running through it, mineral and alive, as if the heron had grown architecture.

The second seam went worse. She pressed too hard and a bead of gold-black epoxy squeezed out along the heron's wing, and she wiped at it and smeared it, and for a moment she sat with her head in her hands. Then she cleaned it as best she could with a cotton swab and let it cure, and the smear stayed, visible, gold-bright, exactly where the wing met the body. It was ugly and it was honest, and she could not tell which of those words her grandmother would use for it.

When her grandmother came in through the back door, smelling of tomato leaves, Anna was sitting at the table with the finished bowl in front of her, turning it slowly with both hands. She did not have a speech prepared, which she understood now was probably correct, since the bowl was the speech. Her grandmother set down the colander she was carrying. She looked at the bowl for a long time without touching it, and Anna watched her take in the gold seams, the heron with its ruined, luminous wing.

"I broke it," Anna said. "This afternoon. I found a way to fix it. Carina told me about it, it's called kintsugi, and I know it's not real gold, and I know I should have told you first."

Her grandmother pulled out the other chair and sat. She turned the bowl a quarter turn, then another, so the light ran down the largest seam, and Anna saw that her grandmother's eyes were wet, though her voice was ordinary when she spoke. "Your grandfather chipped this in Okinawa carrying it in his coat," she said. "I never told you that. I glued the chip so it wouldn't show, and I've been a little ashamed of it for fifty years." She ran her thumb along the gold, over the smeared place on the wing, and left her thumb there. "Show me how you did the powder," she said. "And then help me with the tomatoes, because Mr. Marino has let the stakes lean again and he'll ruin the whole row if we don't go back over there."

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: An arbitration clause requires the parties to settle disputes through private arbitration instead of in court, and in the US it is often paired with a waiver of class-action lawsuits.
story:
Isla had been accepted to three colleges, and all three wanted her answer by the first of May, which was why she was sitting at her mother's desk at ten at night with a bowl of untouched cereal beside the keyboard, opening the financial aid portal for the fourth time. The portal had been updated since her last visit. A banner across the top said that continued use of the site constituted acceptance of the revised terms, and underneath, in smaller gray letters, a link that said View Full Terms and Conditions.

She clicked it the way you click anything at that hour, without hope. The document that loaded was forty-one pages. She scrolled past sections on governing law, on severability, on the apportionment of legal fees if either party sued the other, and then she stopped, because a phrase near the bottom of page twelve caught her eye. It said that by accepting these terms, she agreed to resolve any dispute through binding private arbitration instead of in court. Below that, a second paragraph said she also waived her right to participate in any class-action lawsuit.

She read both paragraphs twice. Somewhere below the window her mother was watching television, and the laugh track rose and fell like a tide. Isla copied the phrase into a search bar, and within a few minutes she understood that this was not some strange feature of one financial aid portal. It was everywhere. Phone apps, streaming services, the food delivery app she had used twice. Every time she had tapped "agree" without reading, she had been signing away a thing she had not known she owned.

She called Cloe, who was still awake because Cloe was always still awake. "Do you know what an arbitration clause is?" Isla asked.

"The thing where you can't sue, you have to do the private judge instead," Cloe said around something crunchy. "My dad complains about them constantly. Why, are you in trouble?"

"No. Maybe. I don't know." Isla explained about the portal, the forty-one pages, the waiver. "So if they messed up my aid, or lost my data, or whatever, I couldn't go to court. Some company person decides."

"That's so bleak," Cloe said, with what sounded like genuine enthusiasm. "It's like signing a contract with a ghost. Anyway, don't you have to accept? It's your financial aid."

That was the part that kept Isla at the desk after the call ended. She could refuse, in theory. There was a mailing address on page thirty where you could supposedly opt out of the arbitration portion by sending a letter within thirty days, an actual paper letter, addressed to a company she could not picture. She imagined her envelope traveling across the country to arrive at some alluvial plain of mailrooms, sliding into a bin, and she imagined the alternative, which was clicking accept and being done, the way she had been done a hundred times before. Her mother would say click it, mija, the school is the school. Her mother had signed leases and hospital forms and employment agreements her whole life in a language she was still learning, and she had never once suggested that the fine print was a place where a person could live.

Isla found the opt-out clause again and read it until she could nearly recite it. Then she opened a new document and began drafting the letter, which felt suddenly invigorating, the way saying no in the right format can feel, even when you are not sure the no will reach anyone. She typed her name, her account number, the words I wish to opt out of the arbitration provision and class-action waiver, and stopped at the signature line. On the screen behind her draft, the portal waited with its patient gray banner, and she understood, with an honesty she did not enjoy, that she could hold both ideas at once: that the letter was a small act of sovereignty, and that it would probably change nothing, and that she was going to send it anyway, tonight, before she lost her nerve.

In the morning she would ask Alaa to read it over, and maybe Mr. Santos, who taught civics and kept a stack of envelopes in his desk drawer for exactly this kind of thing, or so he claimed. For now she printed one page, signed it in blue ink because a website had once told her blue was better, and set it on top of her mother's keys where she could not leave the apartment without it.

"Who are you writing to at midnight?" her mother asked from the doorway, holding a cup of tea.

"The future," Isla said, and slid the letter into an envelope.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: In Darley and Latané's 1968 experiment, about 85 percent of people who thought they alone heard someone having a seizure helped, but only about 31 percent did when they thought four others heard it.
story:
Mr. Wardak had moved the desks into a circle for the seminar, which everyone knew meant participation counted. Jaxon knew it better than most, because he had done none of the reading, and because three nights ago he had stood in the queue at the coffee shop on Ridge Street and watched a man fall sideways off his stool, knocking his cup across the counter, and had done nothing.

It was not that he had wanted to do nothing. The cashier had looked at the door. A woman in a green coat had looked at the counter. Jaxon had looked at the woman in the green coat, and by the time Aleksandar, who had been two places behind him, crouched down and said, "Sir, can you hear me," the man was already blinking and apologizing and asking whether he had to pay for the cup. Jaxon had paid for his own coffee and left, and he had not told anyone he was there, and Aleksandar had not mentioned seeing him.

"Now," Mr. Wardak said, tapping the whiteboard where he had written the word responsibility and underlined it twice. "Kant says you cannot be blamed for what you cannot control. Fine. But most of what we do or fail to do, we could control. So why the gap?"

Joseph, who read everything and highlighted it in four colors, raised his hand halfway, which for Joseph was a full gesture. "There's that experiment. Nineteen sixty-eight, Darley and Latané. They had people talking over intercoms, and one voice starts having a seizure. When subjects thought they were the only one hearing it, about 85 percent went for help. When they thought four other people heard it too, only about 31 percent did."

"That's diffusion of responsibility," Aleksandar said.

"Thirty-one percent," Mr. Wardak repeated, as if tasting it. "Roughly a third of people, each presumably decent, each presumably confident in their own conscience."

Jaxon's throat went dry. He was not sure why his hand went up; it was the same strange mechanism as standing in the queue, except inverted, and he heard himself say, "I was there." The circle turned. "Not in the experiment. At the coffee shop on Ridge, Tuesday night. The guy who fell. I was three feet away and I looked at someone else to check whether it was my job."

"You're making that up to have something to say," said Aleksandar, but not unkindly.

"I wish." Jaxon told it plainly, the cup sliding, the woman in the green coat, the half-second that stretched like taffy. He had spent two nights turning it over, first with the shame people propitiate by promising themselves they will be better, then more usefully, and what he had concluded was that the problem was not a failure of character but a failure of arithmetic. If he had been alone in that shop, he would have moved. He was almost certain of it. Add four witnesses and something in him divided the obligation by five and rounded down to nothing.

"Which is the point of the numbers," Joseph said. "It's not that people in groups are worse people."

"But that's not the whole picture either," Jaxon said, surprising himself again. "Because a rule can't just be 'act first, always.' My dad works in construction, and his whole safety training is the opposite, don't rush in, because the guy who runs to help an electrical hazard becomes the second casualty. Every choice has a trade-off. You want fast action and you want correct action and sometimes you only get one."

"So what's your considered position?" Mr. Wardak asked. "You've given us Kant and your father."

"My position is that the default should be move, and then think while moving. Because the cost of a false alarm is embarrassment, and the cost of the other thing is a man on a floor while five people check each other's faces. But I'm honest that I don't know where the line is. If it's an electrical hazard, moving first is wrong. I can't resolve that into one clean rule, and I don't trust anyone who says they can."

There was a silence of the good kind. Mr. Wardak opened his mouth, and then his mouth kept opening, and a sound came out of him like a hinge, and he began to cough, hard, bent over the desk, his pen clattering onto the floor and rolling in a slow arc toward Jaxon's shoe.

Nobody moved. Joseph looked at Aleksandar. Aleksandar looked at the door, exactly the way the woman in the green coat had looked at the counter.

Jaxon stood up so fast his chair shrieked against the tile, crossed the circle in three steps, and put his hand on Mr. Wardak's back just as the coughing resolved itself into laughter, real laughter, wheezing and unpreventable, and Mr. Wardak straightened, wiped his eyes, and held up the water bottle he had been reaching for the entire time.

"Trachea spasm," he managed. "Happens when I laugh at my own jokes. I was going to fake the collapse for dramatic effect, but you've ruined it, Jaxon. You've absolutely ruined it."

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: During Chuseok, Korea's harvest festival on the 15th day of the eighth lunar month, many families hold charye, a memorial rite that sets out food for their ancestors.
story:
Hudson's grandmother had always been the one who eviscerated the fish, a quick and unceremonious business with the paring knife, and Hudson had never once offered to help. This year she was in a hospital bed across town with her heart doing whatever failing hearts do, and so at nine in the morning on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, it was Hudson who stood at the sink with a sea bream, a knife, and the sinking certainty that he was about to ruin something he could not name.

"You don't have to be perfect," his mother said from the stove, where the rice was coming to a boil. "You just have to do it."

That was the deal they had struck two weeks ago, after the doctor's appointment, when his grandmother had grabbed his wrist in the parking garage and told him it was his turn. He would set the table himself, start to finish, for the whole family. He had agreed the way you agree to anything in a hospital parking garage, quickly, wanting to be elsewhere. Since then he had been calling her in the evenings, taking notes on a legal pad, and the notes were a mess of arrows and corrections, because she kept changing her mind about where the chestnuts went, or he kept asking the wrong questions, or both.

His phone buzzed on the counter. Treyton, from the group chat: you seriously skipping the pickup game for a dinner. Mahmoud had sent only a thumbs down, which somehow stung more. Hudson typed half a reply, deleted it, and turned back to the fish. He made the cut the way she had described it, one long stroke, and it was uglier than hers ever was, but the insides came free.

"It's called charye," his mother said when he asked, for the fourth time that morning, what exactly they were doing. She said it the way she said everything about these things, flatly, as though the word were a coin she was handing over. "The rite. During Chuseok. We set out food for the ancestors." She said it to the rice pot, not to him, and he understood that this was as close to an explanation as she would go. She had grown up watching her mother do it and had never once led it herself; that was a fact he was not supposed to have noticed, and he had noticed it anyway.

The table was the hard part. His grandmother's diagram, dictated over a bad phone line, said the fruit went on the first row, the fish and meat behind it, rice and soup at the far end, but she had said other things too, on other nights, and he had two pages of the legal pad that contradicted each other. At ten o'clock the doorbell rang and it was Ms. Sokolov from next door, holding a plate of shortbread and wearing the expression of someone who had heard, through the walls, an argument about pears. "I won't stay," she said, and stayed forty minutes, standing at the edge of the kitchen being voluble about the weather, the parking on their street, and her own grandmother's cooking, which had apparently been legendary. She had been a raconteur in her day, everyone said so, though today the stories came out in a worried jumble, and Hudson realized halfway through that she was not there for the shortbread or the gossip. She was there because she knew what it was to watch a family try to hold a shape with one person missing.

The family arrived at noon: his father with a bag of tangerines, his aunt already talking, his little cousin already underfoot. Hudson laid out the tablecloth and then stood in front of the empty table with his legal pad, and the room went quiet in a way rooms do when everyone is waiting to see whether you know what you are doing. He set the fruit first. Then the fish, whole, head facing east, which his grandmother had insisted on twice and his aunt disputed once, and his mother settled it with a single look. The rice and soup went at the far end, toward the window, where his grandmother always said the ancestors could find them, though she had never said why the ancestors needed help finding anything, and Hudson had never asked, and now it seemed too late to ask about that particular thing.

He poured the wine last. There was a moment, between setting down the bottle and lifting the cup, when he thought about Treyton and Mahmoud and the pickup game, and about all the evenings he had spent in this kitchen not helping, watching his grandmother's hands move through the same sequence he was now performing badly, and he understood that the two of them had been doing something together for years without either of them calling it that. He could not decide whether it was worse to have missed it or lucky to have caught it before it ended, and he set the problem down the way you set down a heavy bowl, intending to come back for it.

"Is it right?" his cousin whispered.

"Close enough," his aunt said, which from her was practically a benediction.

His mother lit the incense. Then they bowed, all of them, his cousin copying the angle of his father's back, and Hudson held his bow a second longer than he had to, facing the table he had made and the window beyond it and the gray sky over the hospital across town. When he straightened, the smoke was still rising, and his phone buzzed once more in his pocket, and he let it.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: After a LEFT JOIN, COUNT of an orders column gives 0 for customers without orders, but COUNT(*) gives 1, because it counts the NULL-filled row.
story:
The repair shop smelled of flux and burnt coffee, and Owen had claimed the back counter as his desk for the summer. Mr. Rahimi had agreed to pay him under the table for two things: fixing cracked screens and building a database that would tell the shop who its customers were. Three weeks in, the screens went fine. The database did not.

"Same report again," Aaron said, dropping his backpack on a stool. He worked the front counter on Saturdays and had taken to hovering over Owen's laptop during lulls. "The one you said would take an hour."

"It did take an hour." Owen turned the screen toward him. "It's just wrong."

The report claimed that every customer in the shop's records had brought in a repair at least once. Mr. Rahimi knew this was false because he could name people off the top of his head who had never come back after the free estimate, and he wanted those names, since they were the ones worth calling. He had been pithy about it that morning: "Everyone's a customer. Find me the ones who aren't." Owen had a table of customers, a table of repairs, and a query he'd written by copying the shape of something from a tutorial. It joined the two tables and counted, and it insisted on a world where nobody had ever walked away.

He had assumed the join itself was broken. Then he'd assumed the data was dirty, some misspelled name matching nothing. Sage, who was taking the same online course and had finished the module a week early, had looked at his screen on Thursday and said only, "It's not the join," which Owen had found less helpful than she clearly intended. She wasn't being smug. She genuinely thought being told the wrong place to look was a kindness, and he couldn't decide whether he agreed.

Aaron wanted the report for a different reason. He'd been trying to convince Mr. Rahimi to let him run a referral promo, and he needed numbers to argue with, something to slide across the counter on Monday morning. "If you can't tell him who never ordered, I can't tell him who did," Aaron said, tapping the edge of the laptop. "So this is my afternoon too."

"Then sit down and be useless quietly."

Aaron sat. A customer came in with a phone in a sandwich bag, and Aaron quoted her a diagnostic fee while Owen, more to escape the conversation than to advance it, ran the join with nothing else, no counting, just the raw rows. He scrolled. There was Marta Osei, three repairs. There was a man with an unpronounceable street name, one screen replacement. And then there were rows where the customer columns were full and the repair columns were empty, all of them, one long stretch of nulls. The join hadn't failed. It had done exactly what he asked. It had kept the customers with no repairs and padded their side of the row with nothing.

He looked at his original query again. He had written COUNT(*), the way the tutorial had, because the asterisk looked confident and complete. He changed it, on something close to a hunch, to count a column from the repairs side instead, the repair ID. He ran it. Marta Osei's row now read three. And the man with no repairs read zero. Not blank. Zero.

"Ha," Owen said.

"What."

"Look." He turned the laptop. "Same join. I was counting everything the join made, including the padded rows. Every customer got at least one row, so every customer got at least a one. If I count the repair column instead, the empty rows count as nothing. Zero."

Aaron leaned in, reading. "So the report was counting the padding."

"The report was counting the padding." Owen knew there was a sharper way to say it, something Sage would produce instantly, but the blunt version was true and he let it stand. What he didn't know was whether the empty rows were the same as a customer who'd ordered nothing, or whether some of those nulls meant something else, a data problem rather than an absence, and he wasn't sure how to tell. He wrote a note to ask Sage without admitting he hadn't known it himself.

Mr. Rahimi came out from the back with a heat gun in one hand and read the new list over Owen's shoulder. "These people," he said, pointing at the zeros. "Names and numbers by Monday." He went back through the doorway.

"So my promo numbers," Aaron said.

"After the list." Owen was already exporting it, and when Aaron groaned and reached across to scroll the results himself, Owen pulled the laptop an inch out of range and kept typing.
